feed.title: ME/CFS Research Watch
feed.subtitle: New ME/CFS drug trials in Germany and notable new research papers.

entry.title: Paper: Can Depression Polygenic Risk Score Predict Postinfective Fatigue Syndrome (PIFS) in the Dubbo Infection Outcomes Study (DIOS)?
entry.summary:
Researchers followed 464 people after a confirmed infection (like glandular fever) to see who went on to develop postinfective fatigue syndrome (a CFS-like illness after infection) six months later, and tested whether their inherited genetic risk for depression or for chronic fatigue syndrome could predict who would get sick.
Why it matters: Neither genetic risk score predicted the illness overall, pushing back on the idea that post-infective ME/CFS-like illness is really just depression in disguise — though a weak, exploratory hint that depression genetic risk raises the odds in women but lowers them in men needs confirming in a bigger study.
Twin Research and Human Genetics · Ruseva AG, Valencia BM, Gordon SD, et al. https://doi.org/10.1017/thg.2026.10098

entry.title: Paper: Evaluation of an Integrated Multidisciplinary Care Model for Myalgic Encephalomyelitis/Chronic Fatigue Syndrome: A Prospective, Open-label, Non-randomized Controlled Intervention Study
entry.summary:
The Charité Fatigue Center tested a structured care programme for ME/CFS — pacing advice, sleep and pain management, nutrition counselling, social support, and tailored inpatient rehab — against usual single-visit care, following 89 patients on the programme and 93 on usual care for a year.
Why it matters: The extra structured care did not improve patients' physical functioning or other key outcomes after a year, and disability actually got worse for nearly half of the programme group — a disappointing but important negative result showing that good care coordination alone isn't a substitute for an effective medical treatment.
The American Journal of Medicine · Peters CK (formerly published as Kedor C), Mödl L, Rust R, et al. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.amjmed.2026.09.013

entry.title: Paper: Hemodynamic Phenotyping in ME/CFS and ANOCA: Complementary Insights from Coronary Function Testing and Invasive Cardiopulmonary Exercise Testing
entry.summary:
Researchers tested 261 people with unexplained chest pain using detailed heart and blood-vessel tests. 18% of them also had ME/CFS, and 89% of those had "ANOCA" — a condition where the heart's tiniest blood vessels don't work properly even though the main arteries look normal. During exercise, their hearts delivered oxygen normally, but their muscles struggled to use it, pointing to a problem in the muscle rather than the heart.
Why it matters: Diagnosing this small-vessel problem changed how doctors treated 81% of affected patients, suggesting some ME/CFS chest-pain and exercise-intolerance symptoms map onto a specific, already-recognized and testable heart condition — a concrete lead for better diagnosis and management.
American Journal of Physiology-Heart and Circulatory Physiology · Mackay Z, Shah S, Villalobos JG, et al. https://doi.org/10.1152/ajpheart.90080.2026

entry.title: Paper: Clinical Symptomatology, Cognition and Psychosocial Wellbeing in Adolescents With Myalgic Encephalomyelitis/Chronic Fatigue Syndrome: A Cross-Sectional Observational Study
entry.summary:
Researchers in Melbourne compared 25 teenagers with mild-to-moderate ME/CFS to 25 healthy teens. The ME/CFS group's overall intelligence was normal, but they were measurably slower at processing information, and reported much worse sleep, quality of life, anxiety and depression; parents also noticed attention and memory problems.
Why it matters: Shows the "brain fog" many young ME/CFS patients describe is a real, measurable slowdown in mental processing speed rather than lower intelligence — supporting flexible school accommodations rather than assuming affected teens just need to try harder.
Journal of Paediatrics and Child Health · Chau T, Josev EK, Scheinberg A, et al. https://doi.org/10.1111/jpc.70587

entry.title: Paper: Myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome and overlapping post-acute infection syndromes: international expert consensus framework for diagnostic standardization
entry.summary:
19 international ME/CFS experts agreed on a standard way to measure and score seven core symptoms of ME/CFS and related post-infection illnesses (including long COVID) — such as post-exertional malaise (a crash after activity), autonomic problems (trouble with automatic body functions like heart rate or blood pressure), brain fog, and sleep issues — plus a tiered testing plan that avoids unnecessary or risky tests.
Why it matters: A shared, validated way to measure ME/CFS symptoms makes future studies and drug trials easier to compare across different research centers, which is a practical building block for better trial design.
BMC Medicine · Kujawski S, Eaton-Fitch N, Słomko J, et al. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12916-026-05161-8

entry.title: Paper: A systems microbiology framework for reproducible multi-dataset omics integration with application to long COVID
entry.summary:
Researchers built a new computer method to reliably combine several small, messy studies of gene activity in long COVID and found a consistent pattern of seven genes, involved in immune response and energy production, that showed up across different patient groups. They then matched these genes to existing drugs that might be repurposed to treat long COVID.
Why it matters: Gives researchers a shortlist of biological targets and already-approved drugs worth investigating for long COVID, and a reusable method for finding similar signals in related conditions like ME/CFS.
Frontiers in Systems Biology · Varga B, Martinez-Archundia M, Willemsen LEM, et al. https://doi.org/10.3389/fsysb.2026.1873899

entry.title: Paper: Voluntary wheel running behavior is reduced by SARS-CoV-2 S1 administration and mitigates hypothalamic neuroinflammatory processes
entry.summary:
In a rat study, injecting a piece of the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein into the brain fluid made the animals voluntarily exercise less (a stand-in for fatigue), while letting them exercise on their own reduced the brain inflammation that the spike protein had caused.
Why it matters: An animal model directly linking a coronavirus protein to brain inflammation and reduced activity supports the idea that leftover viral material can trigger the kind of brain inflammation thought to drive post-viral fatigue, and hints that some exercise may calm rather than worsen it in this model — a nuance worth watching against reports that exertion harms ME/CFS patients.
Brain, Behavior, & Immunity - Health · Kelley T, Frank MG, Ball JB, et al. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bbih.2026.101331

entry.title: Paper: Gut microbiome signatures during acute infection are associated with long COVID
entry.summary:
In people followed from the time of their original COVID-19 infection onward, the mix of bacteria in their gut measured during that early, acute illness — not afterward — predicted who would go on to develop long COVID, and different bacterial patterns lined up with different symptom patterns.
Why it matters: Suggests a gut-bacteria test taken during the initial infection could one day help flag who is at risk of long COVID, and points to the gut-immune connection as a possible early treatment target.
Gut Microbes · Comba IY, Mars RAT, Yang L, et al. https://doi.org/10.1080/19490976.2026.2718581

entry.title: Paper: The Post-COVID syndrome caused by excessive inflammation: pathogenesis, potential targets and therapeutic agents
entry.summary:
A review article gathering evidence that ongoing, excessive inflammation drives long-COVID fatigue, and cataloguing drugs and other treatments being explored to calm that inflammation.
Why it matters: Provides a roadmap of anti-inflammatory drug candidates that could be tested in future long-COVID and ME/CFS trials.
Frontiers in Pharmacology · Zhou T, Xue G, Zhang Y, et al. https://doi.org/10.3389/fphar.2026.1852220

entry.title: Paper: Subclinical neurovascular and immune correlates of post-COVID-19 syndrome detected by retinal imaging
entry.summary:
Using detailed eye-imaging technology, researchers found subtle changes in the small blood vessels and immune activity at the back of the eye in people with post-COVID syndrome, even when nothing looked obviously wrong on standard exams.
Why it matters: The retina is one of the few places doctors can directly see small blood vessels and nerve tissue, so these subtle changes offer a non-invasive window into the vascular and immune problems that may underlie post-COVID and ME/CFS fatigue.
Brain, Behavior, & Immunity - Health · Wunderle M, Wicklein R, Ribeiro A, et al. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bbih.2026.101315

entry.title: Paper: Effect of low-dose naltrexone for long COVID: a systematic review and meta-analysis
entry.summary:
This review pooled the available studies on low-dose naltrexone (LDN) — a cheap generic drug widely used off-label by long-COVID and ME/CFS patients — to see whether it actually helps with symptoms like fatigue.
Why it matters: LDN is one of the most commonly self-tried treatments in this patient community, so an independent pooled review of the evidence directly informs whether it deserves a proper, dedicated clinical trial.
BMJ Open · Byambasuren O, Atkins T, Baptista S, et al. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjopen-2025-111253

entry.title: Paper: Postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome in adolescents with ME/CFS — a case control study
entry.summary:
Doctors compared 18 teenagers with ME/CFS to 18 healthy teenagers using a simple 10-minute standing test that tracks heart rate and blood pressure. Over a third of the ME/CFS group turned out to have postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS, a condition where the heart races too much on standing up), while none of the healthy teens did — and just looking at how much the heart rate rose during that standing test, without needing an expert exam, identified it almost as well.
Why it matters: Offers a simple, low-cost heart-rate-based test that non-specialist doctors could use to spot a treatable circulation problem (POTS) in teenagers with ME/CFS, potentially speeding up diagnosis and access to treatment.
Frontiers in Pediatrics · Leone A, Gerrer K, Viereck A, et al. https://doi.org/10.3389/fped.2026.1836407

entry.title: Paper: Seven replicated genomic associations of myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome: a biobank study
entry.summary:
Using genetic data from the UK Biobank (about 1,268 people with ME/CFS) and two smaller replication groups, researchers found seven gene regions that show up consistently in ME/CFS, including one (CLYBL) where the ME/CFS-linked gene variant is tied to lower activity of that gene in brain tissue.
Why it matters: Independent replication of specific ME/CFS gene hits (not just single large studies like DecodeME) strengthens the case that ME/CFS has a real, findable genetic and biological basis, and points to genes worth investigating as drug targets.
medRxiv (preprint) · Slaughter J, Labayle O, Roskams-Hieter B, et al. https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.09.09.26362115

entry.title: Paper: Clinical Phenotypes of Post-Acute Sequelae of SARS-CoV-2 (PASC) Infection: A Longitudinal Cohort Study from Karachi, Pakistan
entry.summary:
A year-long study of long-COVID patients in Karachi, Pakistan tracked their symptoms alongside leftover virus detected in stool samples and blood serotonin (a gut/mood signalling chemical) levels. Most symptoms eased over time, but muscle pain, weakness and fatigue persisted in many, and people who still had detectable virus in their stool were more likely to report breathlessness, fatigue, weakness and joint pain.
Why it matters: Adds rare long-term post-viral illness data from South Asia and supports two mechanisms increasingly proposed for ME/CFS-like fatigue — lingering virus in the gut and disrupted serotonin signalling — as possible drivers of persistent symptoms.
medRxiv (preprint) · Khanum I, Ahmed K, Munir T, et al. https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.09.04.26361413

entry.title: Paper: Total blood volume and red blood cell volume are not associated with orthostatic intolerance in adults with myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome
entry.summary:
Researchers measured the actual amount of blood and red blood cells in 49 adults with ME/CFS, then tested how their bodies reacted to standing up (orthostatic intolerance — dizziness, a racing heart, or breathing changes when upright). More than half had an abnormal standing-test result, but whether someone had low, normal, or high blood volume made no difference to who was affected.
Why it matters: Low blood volume has long been suspected as a cause of standing intolerance in ME/CFS; this study suggests it isn't the main driver, pointing instead to nerves, blood vessels, breathing, or brain blood flow as more promising targets for treatment.
Physiological Reports · Yamazaki T, Mancini DM, Blate M, et al. https://doi.org/10.14814/phy2.71087

entry.title: Paper: Exercise Lactate in Post-COVID-19 Condition: Pathophysiological Signal, Phenotyping Tool, or Candidate Biomarker? A Narrative Review with a Hypothesis-Generating Clinical Observation
entry.summary:
This review looks at lactate (a byproduct your muscles make when they can't produce energy efficiently) measured during exercise in people with long COVID, adding the authors' own small case series of 22 patients whose blood lactate at peak exertion was about six times higher than at rest. The review concludes lactate varies too much between people and test methods to diagnose the condition on its own.
Why it matters: Post-exertional malaise (the crash after activity that is a hallmark of ME/CFS) is hard to measure objectively; an exercise-lactate signature is an early candidate for an objective marker of impaired energy metabolism, though this narrative review says it isn't ready for clinical use yet.
Current Problems in Cardiology · Sakellaropoulos SG, Spedicato V, Pfister O https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cpcardiol.2026.103453

entry.title: Paper: Mapping the complexity of ME/CFS: Evidence for abnormal energy metabolism, altered immune profile, and vascular dysfunction
entry.summary:
Comparing blood from ME/CFS patients and healthy people, researchers found several problems at once: immune cells were short on the energy molecule ATP (the cell's fuel), several immune-cell types looked less mature than normal, and blood proteins linked to clotting and blood-vessel reactivity were raised — a sign of blood-vessel (endothelial) dysfunction.
Why it matters: Brings together energy, immune and blood-vessel abnormalities in ME/CFS in one study, and points toward measurable markers that could eventually help diagnose the illness or targets for treatment.
Cell Reports Medicine · Heng B, Gunasegaran B, Krishnamurthy S, et al. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.xcrm.2025.102514

entry.title: Paper: Fatigue is associated with stimulus-related theta and alpha power and distinguishes subjective from objective cognition in a post-viral cohort: A cross-sectional study
entry.summary:
In a large German post-viral cohort, brainwave recordings (EEG) showed that people who felt more fatigued had different patterns of brain activity (theta and alpha waves) during mental tasks, even when their measured performance looked normal.
Why it matters: Offers an objective, brain-based marker for the mismatch between how fatigued someone feels and how they perform on tests — a mismatch that is common and hard to explain in ME/CFS and long COVID.
Research Square (preprint) · Neumann C, Godbersen L, Schmeer L, et al. https://doi.org/10.21203/rs.3.rs-10753262/v1

entry.title: Paper: A distinct effector B cell population drives autoantibody production in SARS-CoV-2 infection
entry.summary:
Studying blood samples from COVID-19 patients, researchers found a specific type of immune cell (a kind of B cell) that makes autoantibodies — antibodies that mistakenly attack the body's own tissues — and identified a signal that switches these cells on.
Why it matters: Autoantibodies are a leading suspect behind symptoms in ME/CFS and long COVID; pinpointing the exact cell type and its trigger gives researchers a specific new target to aim future drugs at.
Immunity · Yuan D, Li S, Zhang R, et al. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.immuni.2026.08.002

entry.title: Paper: Cognition-Linked Monocyte State Reveals Altered Myeloid-Lymphoid Coordination in Neuro-PASC
entry.summary:
In older adults with long-COVID brain fog, researchers found an unusual state of certain white blood cells (monocytes) that coincided with poorer coordination between different parts of the immune system.
Why it matters: Adds to evidence that immune-cell dysfunction, not just direct brain injury, may underlie the fatigue and cognitive problems seen in long COVID and ME/CFS.
International Journal of Molecular Sciences · Hanson BA, Cogswell AC, Lopez M, et al. https://doi.org/10.3390/ijms27167474

entry.title: Paper: Loss of vesicular monoamine transporter 2 in striatum of long COVID and relationship to neuropsychiatric symptoms
entry.summary:
Brain scans of people with long COVID showed fewer working dopamine-releasing nerve endings in a brain region involved in motivation and movement, and the loss lined up with how apathetic, slowed-down, or forgetful people felt.
Why it matters: Points to a specific, measurable brain change behind some long COVID motivation and thinking problems, and suggests boosting dopamine signalling could be worth testing as a treatment.
EBioMedicine · Liu YK, Persaud D, Vieira EL, et al. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ebiom.2026.106339

entry.title: Paper: Acute Protein Responses Control SARS-CoV-2-specific Neurocognitive and General Post-Viral Sequelae
entry.summary:
Researchers tested saliva samples taken soon after a COVID-19 infection and found that people whose bodies made more of certain antiviral immune proteins early on were less likely to develop lasting brain fog and fatigue-type symptoms months later.
Why it matters: A simple, early saliva test might one day flag who is at risk of long-term post-viral fatigue and brain fog, and points to specific immune proteins as possible treatment targets.
medRxiv (preprint) · Liou TG, Andrews RJ, Bass BL, et al. https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.08.27.26361488

entry.title: Paper: Abnormal post-exercise depression of corticomotor excitability is associated with fatigue in post-COVID-19 condition
entry.summary:
Using magnetic pulses to test brain-to-muscle signaling before and after exercise in 58 people with long COVID, researchers found the brain's motor output failed to recover normally after physical effort, and this abnormal pattern matched how fatigued patients said they felt.
Why it matters: Gives doctors an objective, brain-based way to measure post-exertional fatigue instead of relying only on self-reported tiredness, which could help diagnose patients and track treatment response in future trials.
Clinical Neurophysiology · Sebastianelli L, Dezi S, Ortelli P, et al. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.clinph.2026.2112384

entry.title: Paper: Beyond genes: EpiSwitch® and Orion platform-powered 3D genome architecture biomarkers reveal shared biology across ME/CFS, long COVID, PTSD, rheumatoid arthritis, and multiple sclerosis
entry.summary:
Some genes are switched on or off depending on how DNA is folded up in 3D inside the cell, not just by the DNA code itself. Using a technology that reads this 3D folding pattern, researchers compared blood samples from people with ME/CFS, long COVID, PTSD, rheumatoid arthritis, and multiple sclerosis, and found overlapping folding-pattern "fingerprints" shared across these very different-looking illnesses.
Why it matters: Suggests these conditions may share some deeper, measurable biology despite looking different on the surface, and extends the same group's earlier ME/CFS-specific biomarker work (EpiSwitch) into a cross-disease comparison that could eventually help with diagnosis.
Journal of Translational Medicine · Hunter E, Alshaker H, Vugrinec D, et al. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12967-026-08874-9

entry.title: Paper: Uncovering the hidden biology of fibrinaloid microclot complexes in complex, inflammatory diseases
entry.summary:
"Microclots" are unusually tough, hard-to-dissolve blood clots that some researchers think build up in inflammatory illnesses. This review by a leading microclot research group explains how these clots form, why the body struggles to break them down, and how they might cause symptoms in diseases including ME/CFS and long COVID.
Why it matters: Consolidates and extends the microclot/endothelial (blood-vessel-lining) hypothesis that also motivates some ME/CFS and long-COVID treatment ideas, from the research group (Pretorius/Kell) most closely associated with this line of work.
QRB Discovery · Grixti J, Pretorius E, Kell DB https://doi.org/10.1017/qrd.2026.10022

entry.title: Paper: Small extracellular vesicles proteome reveals persistent inflammatory and coagulopathic dysregulation in long-COVID
entry.summary:
In long-COVID patients with fatigue, brain fog and sleep problems, the proteins carried by tiny blood particles called extracellular vesicles showed lasting signs of inflammation and abnormal blood-clotting activity.
Why it matters: Adds another piece of evidence, via a different lab and method, for the inflammation-plus-abnormal-clotting picture in long COVID — the same "microclot" territory as other papers tracked here.
Frontiers in Immunology · Chandran S, Chen L, Ram AK, et al. https://doi.org/10.3389/fimmu.2026.1805159

entry.title: Paper: Associations between multidimensional fatigue and wearable-derived cardio-respiratory variables in post-COVID-19 patients: an observational study
entry.summary:
30 people in post-COVID rehab wore sensors day and night that tracked their heart rate and breathing. Physical tiredness, mental tiredness, and emotional tiredness each lined up with a different pattern in these body signals.
Why it matters: Supports using wrist- or chest-worn sensors as an objective way to track different kinds of fatigue over time — useful for helping patients pace themselves and for measuring whether future treatments actually help.
Frontiers in Digital Health · Adão Martins NR, Annaheim S, Büche D, et al. https://doi.org/10.3389/fdgth.2026.1804993

entry.title: Paper: Symptom-based clusters in people with post-COVID-19 condition (PCC)
entry.summary:
In 1,673 people with post-COVID condition in Germany, researchers grouped patients by their pattern of 14 symptoms (including fatigue) rather than by a single label, and found distinct subgroups that differed in age, sex, and psychological factors.
Why it matters: A large German post-COVID cohort adds to the case that "post-COVID condition" isn't one single illness but several patient subgroups, which matters for tailoring treatment and for how future German trials define who to enroll.
Journal of Translational Medicine · Kuczyk C, Herrmann-Lingen C, Stolz M, et al. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12967-026-08582-4

entry.title: Paper: Low serum selenium combined with SELENOP-autoantibodies are associated with persistent fatigue after SARS-CoV-2 infection
entry.summary:
Selenium is a mineral the body needs, and SELENOP is a blood protein that carries it around. In about 750 adults roughly two years after a COVID-19 infection, people with low selenium levels and antibodies that mistakenly attack SELENOP were more likely to still have fatigue — hinting that a mineral shortage, possibly made worse by the immune system attacking its carrier, might contribute to long-lasting tiredness.
Why it matters: Points to a new, easily measurable biomarker (blood selenium plus SELENOP-autoantibodies) for post-viral fatigue and raises an obvious next question — whether selenium supplementation could help — that could be tested in a trial.
Redox Biology · Schmidt B, Asaad S, Mavarani L, et al. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.redox.2026.104273

entry.title: Paper: Molecular, cellular and network mapping of brain structural deviations in patients with Post-COVID19 syndrome
entry.summary:
Brain scans of 20 people with ongoing tiredness after a mild COVID-19 infection showed subtle thickness changes in certain brain regions — especially areas rich in the same protein the coronavirus uses to enter cells, and areas involved in mood and the brain chemical serotonin.
Why it matters: Gives direct brain-imaging evidence that fatigue can follow even a mild infection, and links it to specific, testable biology (viral-entry receptors, serotonin circuits) that could point to future drug targets.
Brain, Behavior, & Immunity - Health · Martins D, Cai Z, Mariani N, et al. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bbih.2026.101292

entry.title: Paper: Increased Mannosylation of Extracellular Vesicles in Long COVID Plasma as a Binding Target for Galanthus nivalis Agglutinin (GNA) Affinity Resin
entry.summary:
Cells release tiny particles into the blood called extracellular vesicles (EVs), a bit like sealed messages. In long-COVID patients, these EVs carry unusual sugar coatings on their surface. Researchers show a plant-derived sugar-binding material can selectively grab EVs with this coating out of blood — a step toward both a diagnostic test and a way to filter disease-linked particles out of the blood.
Why it matters: From the well-known UCSF LIINC long-COVID research group; opens up both a new biomarker idea and a possible future blood-filtering (apheresis-like) treatment approach, similar in spirit to the immunoadsorption trials already tracked here.
International Journal of Molecular Sciences · Pesqueira Sanchez MA, de Necochea Campion R, Dalhuisen T, et al. https://doi.org/10.3390/ijms27135723

entry.title: Paper: Chronic Fatigue Syndrome in Long COVID: prevalence and impact on health-related quality of life and health status. A cross-sectional study. BioICOPER study
entry.summary:
Among 304 people with long COVID in Spain, a substantial subgroup met older, formal Chronic Fatigue Syndrome criteria. That subgroup had noticeably worse quality of life and overall health than the long-COVID patients who didn't meet those criteria.
Why it matters: Puts a number on how large and how much worse-off the ME/CFS-like subgroup within long COVID is, which matters for how these patients are defined, studied, and prioritised for care and trials.
Research Square (preprint) · Navarro-Cáceres A, Gómez-Sánchez L, Suárez-Moreno N, et al. https://doi.org/10.21203/rs.3.rs-9593874/v1

entry.title: Paper: Pilot longitudinal integrated transcriptomic-metabolomic study reveals immune and metabolic signatures in non-hospitalized healthcare workers with long COVID
entry.summary:
Healthcare workers who developed long COVID after a mild (non-hospitalized) infection, with fatigue and brain fog as their main symptoms, had unusual patterns in their immune-cell genes and blood chemistry compared to co-workers who fully recovered.
Why it matters: Fills a gap in long-COVID biomarker research, which mostly studies people sick enough to be hospitalized — this looks at the milder, more ME/CFS-like presentation that is harder to study but affects far more people.
Frontiers in Cellular and Infection Microbiology · Espín E, Yang C, Shannon CP, et al. https://doi.org/10.3389/fcimb.2026.1808564

entry.title: Paper: Prevalence and Functional Outcomes of Post-Exertional Malaise among Adults with prior COVID-19: Results from a Representative Survey of New York City Residents
entry.summary:
A survey of over 9,600 New York City adults who previously had COVID-19 found that about one in five still gets post-exertional malaise (PEM) -- a crash after physical or mental effort -- and roughly 4% have symptoms lasting long enough to meet ME/CFS criteria.
Why it matters: It's one of the largest population-representative estimates of how common PEM is after COVID-19, and shows it falls hardest on women, transgender/non-binary people, people of color, and people with less education or existing disabilities -- useful evidence for why clinics should screen for PEM routinely.
medRxiv (preprint) · Packard SE, et al. https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.08.31.26356614

entry.title: Paper: Micronutrition as a Therapeutic Strategy for Mitochondrial Dysfunction in Myalgic Encephalomyelitis/Chronic Fatigue Syndrome and Fibromyalgia: A Narrative Review
entry.summary:
This review rounds up evidence that faulty cell energy production (mitochondrial dysfunction) and cell damage from unstable molecules (oxidative stress) contribute to ME/CFS and fibromyalgia, and asks whether nutrients like NAD+ boosters, B-vitamins, magnesium and CoQ10 could help.
Why it matters: It's a plausible, low-risk treatment angle, but the authors themselves say solid trial evidence for these supplements in ME/CFS specifically is still thin and call for dedicated randomized trials.
Nutrients · Abanades S, Fernandez I, Capdevila N, et al. https://doi.org/10.3390/nu18162702

entry.title: Paper: Auditory sensory gating (P50 suppression) as a biomarker of cognitive fatigue in long COVID
entry.summary:
Researchers measured a specific brain-wave response called P50 suppression — how well the brain filters out repeated, unimportant sounds — in 71 people with long-COVID fatigue. People whose brains were worse at this filtering task reported more mental (cognitive) fatigue, even after accounting for depression.
Why it matters: Points to a simple, objective brain-wave measurement that tracks brain-based fatigue independently of mood, which could help build a much-needed objective test for 'brain fog' in long COVID and ME/CFS.
Neuropsychology · Mischke M, Zaehle T https://doi.org/10.1037/neu0001120

entry.title: Paper: Nutraceuticals targeting mitochondrial and oxidative-inflammatory pathways for post-exertional malaise and cognitive impairment in long COVID: a narrative review
entry.summary:
This review pulls together existing research on cell energy production (mitochondria), harmful oxygen byproducts (oxidative stress), and inflammatory signalling molecules to propose that specific vitamins, minerals, and supplements ('nutraceuticals') acting on these pathways could help long-COVID post-exertional malaise (the crash after activity) and brain fog — though this is a proposed framework, not a tested treatment.
Why it matters: Offers a structured, testable roadmap for future nutraceutical trials in long COVID/ME-CFS-type PEM, but it is a hypothesis-generating narrative review with no new patient data of its own, so treat it as a research agenda rather than evidence that a treatment works.
Nutrients · Praet SFE https://doi.org/10.3390/nu18162650

entry.title: Paper: Fragile mitophagy and post-exertional malaise in long COVID: a hypothesis
entry.summary:
This paper proposes a new explanation for why people crash one to three days after activity in long COVID (post-exertional malaise, PEM): damaged mitochondria (the cell's energy factories) get flagged for clean-up, but the clean-up process doesn't finish properly, so leftover mitochondrial debris keeps triggering inflammation long after the activity itself is over.
Why it matters: A plausible new piece for the PEM puzzle — mitochondrial 'clean-up failure' rather than simply low energy — that could in principle be tested with existing lab methods, though it is one author's hypothesis with no new experimental data behind it yet.
Frontiers in Medicine · Groysman R https://doi.org/10.3389/fmed.2026.1905758

entry.title: Paper: Nirmatrelvir-ritonavir for the treatment of long COVID (RECOVER-VITAL): a randomised, placebo-controlled, phase 2 trial
entry.summary:
In this large US trial, 959 adults with long COVID (symptoms lasting 12+ weeks after COVID-19) were randomly given the antiviral drug Paxlovid (nirmatrelvir-ritonavir) or a dummy pill for 15 or 25 days, to test whether hidden leftover virus is driving their symptoms. Whether people mainly had brain fog, dizziness/fast heart rate, or exercise intolerance (a crash after activity), the drug did not work better than placebo on any measure.
Why it matters: This is the largest, most rigorous test yet of the idea that long COVID is caused by virus lingering in the body, and it found no benefit — a disappointing but important result that pushes research toward other explanations and treatments, including for the exercise-intolerance/PEM-type long COVID that overlaps with ME/CFS.
The Lancet Infectious Diseases · Baden LR, Shah NS, Liu STH, et al. https://doi.org/10.1016/S1473-3099(26)00406-8

entry.title: Paper: Cognitive rehabilitation for adults with long COVID: a randomized clinical trial
entry.summary:
In this England-based trial, 78 adults with lasting brain fog after COVID-19 were randomly given either ten weekly one-on-one 'cognitive rehabilitation' sessions (practical coaching on personally chosen everyday goals, like remembering appointments) or usual care. People who got the coaching made significantly more progress on their chosen goals than those on usual care, and much of the benefit was still there six months later.
Why it matters: A well-designed randomized trial — a rarer and stronger type of evidence — showing a real, non-drug treatment can meaningfully help the brain-fog side of long COVID, a symptom with no approved treatment.
JAMA Network Open · Vanova M, Patel AMR, Scott I, et al. https://doi.org/10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2026.20687

entry.title: Paper: Wearable-derived cardiopulmonary fitness and physical activity in adults with long COVID: a RECOVER-Adult digital health substudy
entry.summary:
Using wrist-worn fitness trackers on almost 1,500 people an average of about 21 months after COVID-19, researchers found that those with a high long-COVID symptom burden had lower heart-rate variability at rest, a faster resting heart rate, and were far less physically active day-to-day than those with a low symptom burden — showing the fitness drop is real, measurable, and does not simply fade with time.
Why it matters: Objectively confirms, with wearable data rather than just questionnaires, that long COVID can cause a lasting drop in heart and activity fitness nearly two years out, and raises the question of whether long COVID itself becomes a long-term heart-health risk factor.
JACC: Advances · Vogel JM, Jenkins T, Cerda M, et al. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jacadv.2026.102923

entry.title: Paper: A comparative analysis of computational clustering methods for symptom-based classification of long COVID
entry.summary:
Patient-researchers analysed survey answers from over 6,000 people with long COVID about 162 symptoms, using three different computer clustering methods to sort patients into subtypes. The three methods largely disagreed with each other about what the 'real' subtypes were, suggesting long COVID's symptom pattern is more of a continuous spectrum than a set of clear-cut categories — though people with more overall symptoms consistently also had worse post-exertional malaise (the crash after activity) and were more often women.
Why it matters: A caution flag for the whole field of long-COVID/ME-CFS 'subtyping' research: which subtype a patient gets assigned may depend more on which statistical method a study happens to use than on a real biological grouping — which matters for how future trials pick and interpret patient subgroups.
Oxford Open Immunology · Green TD, McWilliams C, de Figueiredo L, et al. https://doi.org/10.1093/oxfimm/iqag010

entry.title: Paper: Registered interventional trials fail to cover patient-prioritised treatments in Post-COVID condition (PCC)
entry.summary:
Researchers compared 714 registered post-COVID studies (from ClinicalTrials.gov, the German registry DRKS, and the EU registry) against a list of 29 treatments that patients and their doctors say they actually rely on day to day. Only about 1 in 14 of those studies tested any of those patient-favoured treatments. Post-exertional malaise (PEM, the crash after activity that is the hallmark of ME/CFS) was assessed at all in 57 trials, but was the main thing being measured in only 8 of them. Ten common treatment types — for nervous-system regulation problems, allergic-type mast-cell reactions, and certain repurposed nerve drugs — had no registered trial anywhere, and Germany's DRKS registry had zero trials matching any patient-priority treatment.
Why it matters: Backs up, with hard numbers, a pattern this tracker keeps finding: solid drug trials aimed at the ME/CFS-like PEM symptom are rare, especially in Germany. It makes a data-driven case for steering funding — including Germany's new decade-long "Nationale Dekade" research programme — toward the treatments patients and doctors already believe help, rather than only mechanism-focused studies.
Research Square (preprint) · Gabriel M, Koster S, Puta C, et al. https://doi.org/10.21203/rs.3.rs-10851936/v1

entry.title: Paper: A Multivariable Plasma Extracellular Vesicle Surface Profile Associated with Post-COVID-19 Syndrome
entry.summary:
Blood and spinal-fluid samples from 61 people with lasting post-COVID symptoms, 80 fully recovered people, and 10 people with fatigue after other infections were tested for extracellular vesicles (EVs) — tiny particles cells release into the blood, a bit like sealed messages — looking at proteins on their surface. No single surface protein reliably told the groups apart on its own, but a computer model combining small differences across many proteins together could distinguish post-COVID patients from recovered people reasonably well, and this combined "EV score" dropped back down a year later in patients who improved.
Why it matters: Adds a new type of candidate blood test for post-COVID syndrome — based on particles cells shed, rather than antibodies or hormones — from the same Ulm University team already tracked here for finding no unusual brain immune activity in these patients. Together, the two findings point research away from classic autoimmune brain inflammation and toward other biology (e.g. how cells communicate) as a driver of lasting symptoms.
medRxiv (preprint) · Erhart DK, Ressin H, Balz LT, et al. https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.08.27.26361498

entry.title: Paper: Plasma Proteomics Identifies a Microtesla Magnetic Therapy Response Signature in Long COVID
entry.summary:
In a small trial of a gentle, at-home, whole-brain magnetic-field treatment ("Microtesla Magnetic Therapy") for long-COVID brain fog, some treated patients' thinking and symptoms improved. Researchers then measured over 11,000 blood proteins before and after treatment and found a pattern of about 17 proteins that changed specifically in people who got better, including one protein that normally puts the brakes on a cell-signalling pathway (called Hedgehog signalling) tied to inflammation and tissue repair — suggesting the treatment may work partly by calming inflammation.
Why it matters: Offers early molecular evidence that a non-drug, brain-stimulation approach can produce a measurable biological change in long COVID, and flags specific blood proteins that could help predict who will respond to this or similar treatments — though this is a small feasibility study, not a definitive trial.
medRxiv (preprint) · Brady NR, Canori A, Maltz D, et al. https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.08.25.26361319

entry.title: Paper: Early HHV-6 IgG and IgA responses during acute SARS-CoV-2 infection in relation to long COVID: a multicohort observational study
entry.summary:
Researchers measured antibodies against a very common dormant virus most people already carry (HHV-6, a herpesvirus) in blood drawn right when people first caught COVID-19. One antibody pattern (high 'IgA' antibody against HHV-6) at that early point was linked to a higher chance of later developing long COVID, while a different pattern ('IgG' antibody) was linked to a lower chance.
Why it matters: Adds evidence that a dormant, usually-harmless virus 'waking up' around the time of the original infection may help set someone up for long COVID/ME-CFS-like illness, and hints at an early blood test that might one day flag who is at risk before symptoms even start.
EBioMedicine · Choudhury A, Burry MJ Jr, Kwon WJ, et al. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ebiom.2026.106455

entry.title: Paper: VSL#3® supplementation improves fatigue in long COVID: results from the DELong#3 randomized placebo-controlled trial
entry.summary:
In this Italian trial ('DELong#3'), 48 adults with lasting fatigue after COVID-19 took either a high-dose multi-strain probiotic (a supplement of live gut bacteria, brand VSL#3®) or a placebo (dummy pill) for four weeks. People on the probiotic reported a much bigger drop in their fatigue than those on placebo, and the improvement was still there a month after they stopped taking it.
Why it matters: It's one of the few placebo-controlled trials to show a measurable fatigue benefit in long COVID, and points to the gut microbiome (the community of bacteria living in the intestines) as a plausible, low-risk treatment target — though the trial is small and needs to be repeated in more people.
British Journal of Biomedical Science · Amoroso C, Marinoni B, Maragno P, et al. https://doi.org/10.3389/bjbs.2026.16993

entry.title: Paper: eNOS Uncoupling, Shear-Stress Tolerance, and the Two-Threshold Model of Post-Exertional Malaise in Long COVID: A Mechanistic Hypothesis With Implications for Physiotherapy and Recovery Protocols
entry.summary:
This paper is a theory piece (not a study with new patients) about post-exertional malaise (PEM, the crash after activity) in some long-COVID patients whose blood vessels look normal on standard scans. The authors propose that COVID-19 damages the inner lining of blood vessels in a way that uses up a helper molecule the body needs to make nitric oxide, a gas that normally helps blood vessels relax and handle the extra blood flow during activity. Without enough of that helper molecule, the same machinery that should make nitric oxide instead makes harmful byproducts, which the authors think build up during and after exertion and trigger the crash.
Why it matters: Offers a specific, testable blood-vessel-based explanation for PEM, different from the muscle-calcium theory (Klaus Wirth's hypothesis) or nervous-system theories already tracked here, and suggests concrete before/after-exercise blood tests that could check whether it's right. It also suggests too much rest, not only too much activity, could worsen blood-vessel function — relevant to how patients are advised to pace themselves.
Microcirculation · Karipidis YK, Karipidis KY https://doi.org/10.1111/micc.70082

entry.title: Paper: Acupressure and Qigong in post-infectious fatigue with impaired physical function: a randomized clinical trial
entry.summary:
In this Charité-led trial ('ACUQiG'), 235 people with lasting fatigue and reduced physical functioning after an infection (mostly post-COVID) were split into two groups: one did 8 weeks of daily self-applied acupressure (pressing on specific body points, about 18 minutes a day) plus twice-weekly online Qigong (a gentle mind-body exercise), while the other just got a self-care information leaflet. On the main measure — physical functioning — the acupressure/Qigong group scored a bit higher after 8 weeks, but the difference was too small to be statistically certain it wasn't due to chance. A separate fatigue scale did show a small, statistically real improvement in the treatment group.
Why it matters: A rigorously tested complementary-medicine approach, run by Carmen Scheibenbogen's own Charité group, came back essentially negative on its main goal of restoring physical function — useful, honest evidence for tempering expectations about this kind of non-drug approach, even though it showed a small effect on fatigue specifically.
Frontiers in Medicine · Dietzel J, Bauer T, Tissen-Diabaté T, et al. https://doi.org/10.3389/fmed.2026.1872035

entry.title: Paper: Central noradrenergic deficiency in post-infectious chronic fatigue: neurobehavioral correlates
entry.summary:
Researchers at the US National Institutes of Health tested spinal fluid from 16 people with ME/CFS, 34 with long COVID, 32 with Parkinson's disease (included for comparison, since it's a known noradrenaline-system disease), and 40 healthy volunteers, looking at two brain chemical messengers: noradrenaline (which drives alertness and the body's 'fight or flight' response) and dopamine. People with ME/CFS had clearly lower noradrenaline activity than healthy people — even lower than the long-COVID and Parkinson's groups — while their dopamine levels were normal. This noradrenaline shortfall was linked to weaker hand-grip endurance, worse general health, and was even lower in those who experience post-exertional malaise (PEM, a crash after activity).
Why it matters: Identifies a specific, measurable brain-chemical shortfall in ME/CFS, distinct from a general 'stress' response, and ties it directly to muscle fatigability and symptom severity. The authors suggest it may happen because making noradrenaline costs cells more energy than an ME/CFS-affected 'energy crisis' can supply — offering a concrete, testable mechanism and a possible new drug target (boosting noradrenaline signalling).
Brain Communications · Aregawi L, Walitt B, Sullivan P, et al. https://doi.org/10.1093/braincomms/fcag173

entry.title: Paper: Orthostatic Dysfunction and Myalgic Encephalomyelitis/Chronic Fatigue Syndrome: A Close Reciprocal Relationship Beyond Cardiac Preload Failure and Hypoperfusion
entry.summary:
Standing up puts extra strain on the body, and people with ME/CFS often feel worse when upright (orthostatic intolerance). This paper argues that standing doesn't just strain the heart and blood vessels — it may also directly overload muscle cells with calcium, the same overload process Klaus Wirth has proposed causes post-exertional malaise (PEM, a crash after activity).
Why it matters: Proposes that simply standing — not only physical exertion — could trigger PEM-like crashes in severely ill ME/CFS patients through one shared cellular mechanism, tying together two of the illness's most disabling symptoms; it's Wirth's own hypothesis, so high priority to watch for follow-up evidence.
Preprints.org (preprint) · Wirth KJ https://doi.org/10.20944/preprints202608.1772.v1

entry.title: Paper: Persistent Hypercoagulability and Further Characterization of Microclot Complexes in Long COVID
entry.summary:
Blood was tested from 20 people with long COVID and 19 healthy people. The long-COVID patients' blood clotted faster and firmer than normal (called hypercoagulability), and contained more 'microclots' — tiny clumps of a misfolded blood protein that special dyes can detect sticking to them.
Why it matters: Adds more detailed evidence for the microclot theory of long COVID and ME/CFS — the idea that abnormal, hard-to-dissolve clots clog small blood vessels and starve tissues of oxygen, from Etheresia Pretorius's group, the lab most associated with this research direction.
medRxiv (preprint) · Nunes M, Pereira Guerreiro CM, Pretorius JH, et al. https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.08.20.26360874

entry.title: Paper: Persistent Mitochondrial and Endothelial Dysfunction in Non-Hospitalized Patients with Long COVID
entry.summary:
32 long-COVID patients in Japan were followed for 6 months. Two blood markers — one showing stress in the cell's 'power plants' (mitochondria) and one showing damage to the lining of blood vessels — stayed high in patients who hadn't gotten better, but dropped in those who improved. 91% of participants had fatigue as a main symptom.
Why it matters: The authors directly link these findings to ME/CFS, arguing the same mitochondrial and blood-vessel problems seen here likely underlie ME/CFS fatigue too, and offer a simple blood test for tracking who stays stuck in prolonged illness.
Frontiers in Medicine · Ono R, Takayama S, Abe M, et al. https://doi.org/10.3389/fmed.2026.1921822

entry.title: Paper: Circulating MicroRNA ratios as diagnostic biomarkers for long COVID with an independent validation cohort
entry.summary:
Medical University of Vienna researchers tested blood from 206 long-COVID patients and 71 healthy people, looking at ratios of tiny genetic messenger molecules (microRNAs) linked to mitochondrial and blood-vessel health. Two of these ratios were reliably lower in long-COVID patients in two separate patient groups, though the test's accuracy dropped when checked against an outside dataset.
Why it matters: A step toward an objective blood test for long COVID that could plausibly extend to ME/CFS diagnosis, though the authors are upfront that it isn't accurate enough yet for clinical use.
Communications Medicine · Han E, Lukovic D, Müller-Zlabinger K, et al. https://doi.org/10.1038/s43856-026-01854-6

entry.title: Paper: EBV Reprograms B Cells in an Autoimmune-Like Fashion in Patients with COVID-19
entry.summary:
In COVID-19 patients, the Epstein-Barr virus (EBV, a common 'sleeper' virus most people already carry) can reawaken and reprogram the immune cells it infects (B cells) to act as if they're attacking the body's own tissue. People with more of these reprogrammed cells had worse lingering symptoms 2-3 months later.
Why it matters: EBV reactivation is a long-standing suspect in both long COVID and ME/CFS; this gives a specific cellular mechanism — autoimmune-like B-cell reprogramming — for how a reawakened 'sleeper' virus could drive lasting illness.
bioRxiv (preprint) · Chen DG, Yuan D, Su Y, et al. https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.08.17.745245

entry.title: Paper: A cardiometabolic perspective on post-exertional malaise in myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome (ME/CFS) and Long COVID
entry.summary:
This opinion article argues that post-exertional malaise (PEM, the crash after activity that is the hallmark of ME/CFS) isn't just one system flaring up, but a breakdown in how the heart, blood vessels and metabolism coordinate with each other in the hours and days after exertion — especially in patients who also have obesity or type 2 diabetes.
Why it matters: Proposes a broader way of studying and eventually treating PEM by tracking the heart and metabolism together over time after exertion, rather than looking at one body system at a time — a framework that could help design better drug trials aimed specifically at PEM.
Cardiovascular Diabetology · Westermeier F, Pretorius E, Untersmayr E, et al. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12933-026-03316-8

entry.title: Paper: Microvascular remodeling and endothelial dysfunction across the post-COVID-19 spectrum: a prospective observational case-control study
entry.summary:
Using a special camera that watches how the tiny blood vessels at the back of the eye react to a flickering light, researchers compared 96 healthy people, 102 people who recovered fully from COVID-19, and 102 people with lasting post-COVID symptoms (62 of whom met full ME/CFS criteria). The vessels of post-COVID patients widened less in response to the flicker and were narrower at rest, and this problem was worst in the ME/CFS group, whose blood also showed higher levels of markers linked to inflamed, damaged blood-vessel walls.
Why it matters: Offers a simple, non-invasive eye test as a way to spot and measure the blood-vessel problems thought to underlie ME/CFS, which could help diagnose patients earlier and track whether future vascular-targeted treatments are actually working.
BMC Medicine · Wallraven T, Günthner R, Lethen I, et al. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12916-026-05144-9

entry.title: Paper: Neuroendocrine signature of ME/CFS: Meta-analytic evidence for bioactive cortisol deficit and exaggerated feedback sensitivity
entry.summary:
The body's main stress hormone, cortisol, is made and controlled by a chain of glands called the HPA axis (hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis). Pooling 46 earlier studies (about 1,400 ME/CFS patients vs 1,350 healthy people), researchers found ME/CFS patients consistently have lower cortisol in their saliva, urine and hair, respond more weakly when given a hormone that should trigger a cortisol surge, and suppress their cortisol too strongly when given a steroid that should dampen it slightly.
Why it matters: Points to a genuinely blunted, over-braked stress-hormone system in ME/CFS — not just 'stress' in the everyday sense — that could help explain the poor sleep, brain fog, and low resilience to physical or emotional strain patients report, and gives researchers a measurable target (cortisol testing) to explore for future treatments.
Molecular Psychiatry · Woo TW, Choi YJ, Kim JY, et al. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41380-026-03608-1

entry.title: Paper: Altered TRPM3-Dependent Cytosolic and Mitochondrial Calcium Influx in Natural Killer Cells of Post-COVID-19 Condition Patients
entry.summary:
Researchers looked at natural killer (NK) cells — a type of immune cell — in 8 people with long-lasting post-COVID illness and 8 healthy people. The patients' NK cells had a faulty calcium "gate" (a channel called TRPM3): too little calcium got into the main body of the cell, but too much built up inside the cell's energy-making parts (mitochondria), and the cells barely responded when stimulated.
Why it matters: The same faulty TRPM3 calcium channel was first found in ME/CFS immune cells, so finding it again in post-COVID illness supports the idea that ME/CFS and post-COVID share a common underlying immune and energy problem — a possible shared target for future treatments.
European Journal of Immunology · Magawa CT, Eaton-Fitch N, Muraki K, et al. https://doi.org/10.1002/eji.70240

entry.title: Paper: Investigation of BOLD signal intensities in long COVID patients using 7T functional MRI
entry.summary:
Using an extra-powerful (7 Tesla) brain scanner, researchers compared brain activity in 19 people with long COVID and 27 healthy people while they did a thinking task. The long-COVID patients had weaker brain-activity signals in the regions that handle attention and error-checking, and this was linked to slower thinking and more pain.
Why it matters: Gives high-resolution evidence that long-COVID brain fog and fatigue come with real, measurable changes in brain activity, rather than just being tiredness — from a group that also studies ME/CFS brain imaging, strengthening the case for a shared biological basis.
Brain, Behavior, & Immunity - Health · Inderyas M, Thapaliya K, Marshall-Gradisnik S, et al. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bbih.2026.101266
